# Algorithms should make sense before they become code

An algorithm is useful when you can explain three things:

1. **Why is the obvious solution doing unnecessary work?**
2. **What fact allows the better solution to skip that work without missing an answer?**
3. **How do the formula, a small numerical example, and the program express the SAME decision?**

This library has **73 reworked topic chapters**, but it is **not meant to be read as 73 isolated definitions**. Follow the learning path below first; return to the complete topic catalogue when a problem needs a particular structure.

::: {.callout-important}
## Every equation must be immediately understandable

The writing standard is **plain-English meaning → one equation → explanation of every symbol → substitution with actual numbers → correctness argument → code**. A bare formula with no numeric example is not an acceptable finished lesson. Start with [Read Every Mathematical Symbol](guides/read-the-math.qmd).
:::

## Four foundations to read first

1. [**Read Every Mathematical Symbol**](guides/read-the-math.qmd) — learn $\sum$, $\in$, $\forall$, indexing, recurrences, asymptotic notation and graphs from tiny arithmetic examples.
2. [**How to Choose the Right Algorithm**](guides/choose-a-pattern.qmd) — discover why Sliding Window works on some sums but fails for negative values; compare DP, greedy, graph and search methods.
3. [**How to Prove Correctness and Count Work**](guides/prove-and-count.qmd) — CLRS-style loop invariants, induction, greedy exchange proofs, recurrence trees and amortised analysis.
4. [**CLRS Fourth-Edition Reading Roadmap**](guides/clrs-roadmap.qmd) — follow the MIT Press textbook structure while keeping useful LeetCode topics clearly labelled.

## Begin with eight connected topics

1. [**Sliding Window**](sliding-window/index.qmd) — A changing substring shares nearly all its content with the previous substring. Preserve the valid interval.
2. [**Prefix Sum**](prefix-sum/index.qmd) — Repeated subarray sums share earlier additions. Store cumulative sums and subtract.
3. [**Binary Search**](binary-search/index.qmd) — Sorted input lets one comparison reject half the search interval. Preserve the boundary invariant.
4. [**Backtracking**](backtracking/index.qmd) — All solutions form a decision tree: choose, explore, undo. Learn why undo restores sibling branches.
5. [**Dynamic Programming**](dynamic-programming/index.qmd) — The same subproblem reappears. Define a state and a recurrence instead of re-solving it.
6. [**Greedy**](greedy/index.qmd) — An attractive local choice is safe only if an exchange argument establishes optimality.
7. [**Breadth-First Search**](breadth-first-search/index.qmd) — FIFO exploration finds minimum-hop routes in an unweighted graph.
8. [**Shortest Path**](shortest-path/index.qmd) — Weighted travel times need distance relaxation; minimum-hop paths need not be cheapest.

Study one topic completely before moving to the next. After reading, close the page and explain the example aloud with your own numbers.

## A small demonstration: why input assumptions choose the technique

Suppose the array is **[1,−1,0]**. How many nonempty contiguous subarrays add to zero? The answer is **three**, but a simple shrinking window based on nonnegative sums is not trustworthy here.

We can write every prefix sum, and recognise that a zero-sum interval starts and ends at two **equal** prefix values.

$$
\operatorname{sum}(l, r) = P_r - P_l
$$

where:

- $P_j$ is the sum of the first $j$ elements, with $P_0 = 0$;
- $l$ is the inclusive start index and $r$ the exclusive end index of the subarray;
- $\operatorname{sum}(l, r)$ is the total of the elements from index $l$ up to, but not including, $r$.

Example: the prefixes of $[1, -1, 0]$ are $P = [0, 1, 0, 0]$. Equal prefix pairs give $[1, -1]$ (from $P_0$ to $P_2$), $[1, -1, 0]$ ($P_0$ to $P_3$) and $[0]$ ($P_2$ to $P_3$). Each difference is $0 - 0 = 0$, so the answer is 3.

The formula tells us **what to remember**: counts of earlier prefix sums. That leads directly to the code in [Hash Table, interview problem 2 (LeetCode 560)](hash-table/index.qmd#interview-problems), not the other way around.

## Run your own experiments

Every topic folder has one Java lab next to its lesson, for example [`hash-table/HashTableLab.java`](hash-table/HashTableLab.java). It needs only a JDK (Java 21 or newer). Each lab checks every number its lesson quotes and prints `OK`:

~~~bash
cd algorithms/hash-table
java HashTableLab.java
~~~

Every Java block in a lesson is an exact excerpt of its lab, so the code you read is the code that is tested. [How the labs work, and a list of all of them](examples/index.qmd).

## Source and originality

The book structure and proof-oriented methodology were checked against [MIT Press, *Introduction to Algorithms*, 4e](https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/) and its [official table of contents](https://mitp-content-server.mit.edu/books/content/sectbyfn/books_pres_0/11599/4e_toc.pdf). Patterns and common counterexamples were cross-checked against publicly available [LeetCode community discussions about subarrays](https://leetcode.com/discuss/post/7077374/), [binary search](https://leetcode.com/discuss/post/2371234/) and [dynamic programming](https://leetcode.com/discuss/post/1747722/).

These lessons **do not copy the textbook or community solutions**. Each explanation, numerical substitution and reusable code example is independently written.

[Original topic catalogue metadata](leetcode-topic-catalog.json).
